he last leaf of autumn vanished before Aranion’s eyes—not fallen, but unmade, its outline a heartbeat of gold after-image against the dawn.
So too went his great-grandson’s daughter, a child of seventy summers—barely toddling in elven time—whose laughter had ricocheted through the oak halls only the night before. One instant she chased fireflies; the next, the air closed over her like calm water, and the memory of her weighed more than her body ever had.

Aranion felt the hollow spread upward through the bloodline, a tide eating the youngest sand first. In three days the plague would reach his granddaughter; in seven, his daughter; in nine, himself. A family unwritten in reverse, until the name “Aranion” was a syllable no tongue could shape.

He knew the taste of that magic—velvet smoke, bruised roses, the copper of lust repaid.
Lilindra.

He had left her human-ripe and swelling with his seed three centuries ago, promising to return once he’d “settled affairs” among immortals. She had screamed that every hour of gestation would be a knot in his fate. He had kissed her tears, thinking time an endless spool he could rewind at leisure.

Now the knots were untying themselves, children dissolving like salt in rain.

He found her in the ruins of Veyr, where mortals once nailed offerings of seed and silk to her door. She sat on a broken bedframe, wings furled into a mourning shawl, hair the color of midnight milk. Between her fingers she spun a spindle of glass; within its bulb floated miniature faces—his descendants—fading like candle wicks.

“You kept the line alive,” she said without looking up. “I keep the line erased. Fair trade.”

“Stop it.” His voice cracked like frostbitten metal. “Kill me, not them.”

She lifted her gaze. Her eyes were galaxies imploding.
“I tried. The curse refused. It wants your grief, not your death. It wants you to watch the future unspool until the day your own mother forgets the push that birthed you.”

Aranion dropped to his knees, centuries of dignity sloughing away. “I was a coward. But they are innocent.”

“Innocent of you, perhaps. Not of me.” A tear slid between her breasts, steaming where it touched. “Every night I felt them—heartbeats in parallel wombs while I miscarried memories. You gave me motherhood in abstentia. Now I return the gift.”

He crawled forward, palms bleeding on stone shards. “Then let me feel them too. Let me carry the erasure backward through my own flesh. Give me their vanishing, hour by hour, until nothing remains of Aranion but the space where a father should have been.”

The spindle slowed.
“You would become the void that swallows your name?”

“Yes.” His forehead touched her knees. “Let the last thing I see be your face, and the first thing you forget be mine.”

Silence pooled, thick as anniotic fluid.
Then her wings unfurled, scattering starlight. She pressed the spindle to his chest; glass became water, sinking through ribs. Cold flooded him, intimate as conception reversed.

One by one the faces brightened, rekindling. Out in the world, a toddler’s giggle reinscribed itself upon morning air.

Aranion’s reflection, however, guttered. Skin transluced to parchment, then to space between stars. He felt memories peel—first the scent of his mother’s hair, then the color of sunrise, then the sound of his own voice calling Lilindra’s name.

She caught the final syllable on her tongue, kissed it into nothing.

When the last echo dissolved, the spindle lay empty.
She stood alone, cradling absence the way she once cradled hope, and for the first time in three hundred years the wind carried no echo of him.

Somewhere, children danced beneath oaks that remembered neither betrayer nor savior—only the green sound of continuance.
